<explanation>
Based on both the file tree and README content, this project is a full-stack quantitative stock analysis and trading system. It is designed to fetch daily stock data, calculate technical indicators, perform pattern recognition, enable stock selection/backtesting, and even support automatic trading. In addition, there’s a web layer for visualization and a set of scheduled jobs (via cron scripts and job modules) for data processing. Here’s how to structure a detailed system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Data Acquisition & Crawling: Represent the set of “crawling” modules under instock/core/crawling (which fetch stock details, ETF data, historical trade dates, etc.) to show how the system ingests raw market data.
   • Data Processing & Analysis: Include components for indicator calculations (in instock/core/indicator), K-line and pattern recognition (instock/core/kline and instock/core/pattern), and backtest modules (instock/core/backtest). Also illustrate the “strategy” submodule that encapsulates various stock selection logics.
   • Job Scheduling: Display a scheduler module or a “Job Runner” box representing the instock/job directory (with scripts like execute_daily_job.py, basic_data_daily_job.py, and others) which triggers batch operations on a daily or interval basis. Also show the “cron” directory that contains daily, hourly, and workday scripts.
   • Trading and Execution: Diagram the trade module—particularly instock/trade/robot and related strategy scripts—in which automatic trading logic, event handling, and broker-specific integrations are contained.
   • Web Presentation: Represent the front-end web module (instock/web) that includes static resources, templates, and the web service handler. This component exposes dashboards and data views to the user.
   • Database & Storage: Include a database/data persistence layer that is accessed via modules in instock/lib/database and configured under instock/config. This component stores historical data, indicators, and logs.
   • External Dependencies & Deployment:
       - Docker and Containerization: Outline the “docker” folder and related Dockerfiles plus GitHub workflows, indicating that the system is deployed in Docker containers (with links for development and deployment).
       - TA-Lib and Third-Party Libraries: Represent external libraries such as TA-Lib, pandas, and the various Python dependencies.
       - Broker/Trading Client Integration: Show the integration point for the trading broker (configured with trade_client.json and corresponding trade services).
   • Logging & Supervisor: Mention that there are separate log files for data jobs (stock_execute_job.log), web services (stock_web.log), and trade services (stock_trade.log). Also, supervisor configurations are present to manage daemon processes.

2. Show Relationships and Interactions:
   • Indicate that the Job Scheduler (cron jobs and job scripts) triggers the Data Acquisition and Data Processing components periodically.
   • Display directional arrows from the Data Acquisition component to the Processing & Analysis layer, as raw data is collected and then fed into technical analysis/calculations.
   • Have arrows from the Processing layer to the Database, where computed results (like technical indicators, backtest outcomes, and strategy signals) are stored.
   • Indicate that the Web Presentation layer retrieves data from the Database for visualization.
   • Draw an interaction from the Processing and Strategy modules directly into the Trading component to signal buy/sell decisions.
   • Display integration lines from the entire system to the external Docker/Deployment environment, emphasizing that the system is containerized and uses CI/CD workflows (.github/workflows).
   • Optionally, include a feedback loop from logging and monitoring components back to the system infrastructure for error handling and debugging.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Separation of concerns: Different folders and modules clearly separate data acquisition, processing, trading, and user interface.
   • Modular design: Each functionality (e.g., crawling, indicators, strategies) is encapsulated in its own submodule – an important pattern making the system scalable.
   • Batch processing: The job scheduling and cron script implementation are a key pattern for periodic processing.
   • Multi-threading and singleton design: Note in the README that the system employs multi-thread and singleton patterns for efficiency; these can be noted near the processing modules.
   • Containerization and deployment automation using Docker and GitHub workflows.

4. Tailoring the Diagram to the Project Type:
   • As a full-stack application, split the diagram into logical layers:
       - “Backend Processing & Data Services” (encompassing crawling, indicator calculation, strategy selection, backtesting, and trade engine)
       - “Scheduling & Automation Layer” (representing cron scripts and job runners)
       - “Database & Persistence Layer”
       - “Web Presentation & User Interaction” (representing web service, static assets, and templates)
       - “External Integration” (Docker deployment, broker integration, third-party libraries, and external TA-Lib dependency)
   • Use different colors or shapes to differentiate between these layers and:
       - Label each component with clear names (e.g., “Data Crawler”, “Indicator Engine”, “Backtesting Engine”, “Trade Execution Engine”, “Web UI”).
       - Draw directional arrows to show the data flow (such as “raw data ingested” from Crawling → “processed data stored” in Database → “visualized” in Web UI).
       - Emphasize dependencies like the connection to external trading brokers and TA-Lib.

5. Guidelines for a Detailed Diagram:
   • Ensure each box is clearly labeled with the corresponding module or folder (for example, “instock/core/strategy” or “instock/trade/robot”).
   • Use arrows to show control flow:
       - For instance, arrows from cron -> job scripts -> data processing modules.
       - Arrows from data processing modules -> logging subsystem.
       - Arrows from processing and strategy modules to trade execution.
   • Consider color coding:
       - Use one color for core computational modules (crawling, indicators, strategies, backtesting).
       - A different color for scheduling/job modules.
       - Another for presentation (web) components.
       - Separate colors or shapes for external dependencies (database, Docker, broker integration).
   • Add annotations or call-outs to highlight key design principles such as “modular design”, “batch processing”, and “containerized deployment”.
   • Represent ancillary components like configuration files (instock/config) and the deployment scripts (docker/Dockerfile, supervisor, GitHub CI workflows) to show how automated build, deploy, and logs collection are integrated into the system’s lifecycle.

By organizing the diagram according to the system’s primary responsibilities and the rich modular structure represented in the file tree and README, the principal software engineer can get a clear overview of the entire architecture. This detailed diagram will aid in understanding component responsibilities, interactions, and facilitate more effective system maintenance and evolution.
</explanation>
